narrativeReportMd:
# List R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`List` has a hard local compatibility break centered on `List.subject`: R6 changes it from a singleton `Reference` to a repeating `Reference`, which changes JSON shape from an object to an array for populated instances. R6 also broadens `List.subject` and `List.source` target resource types and removes two R4 mode-dependent entry constraints, creating R6→R4 representability and runtime/semantic risks.

## Scope
I analyzed the R4 and R6 core StructureDefinitions for `List`, related local List ValueSets/CodeSystems, package indexes, package metadata, and the batch manifest entry. I excluded inherited-only base changes such as `DomainResource.language`, base `dom-*` constraints, and base extension behavior.

## Main migration themes
The dominant migration theme is widening: R6 allows more subjects, broader subject target types, broader source author target types, and more combinations of entry metadata with list modes. Widening is usually not R4→R6 validation-breaking in the abstract model, but the `subject` max change is special because FHIR JSON uses different wire shapes for singleton and repeating elements. Down-conversion from R6 to R4 is lossy or invalid for multiple subjects, non-R4 subject/source targets, and entries using `deleted` or `date` outside the old R4 mode rules.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact finding is `List:SERIALIZATION_OR_CODEGEN:List.subject:6b3f2a`, because populated R4 JSON with `subject` as an object is not R6 JSON shape; generated APIs also change from a single property to a collection. `List:REFERENCE_TARGET:List.subject:4aa218` has security and compartment implications because R6 explicitly allows multiple subjects and any resource target.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for multiple-subject access-control behavior and for semantics of `entry.deleted` outside `mode=changes`. The computable definitions show the changes, but the supplied inputs do not include ballot rationale or narrative pages explaining the intended operational behavior.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most widening changes could have been made less disruptive by adding parallel optional elements, profiles, or cross-version extensions while preserving the old base shape. The tradeoff would have been a more complex model and weaker uniform support for multi-subject and broader-author Lists.

## Follow-up analysis
Search parameters, compartment rules, DomainResource inherited changes, and external terminology packages should be reviewed separately before a production migration plan is finalized.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `List` retains the same identity, but R6 changes `List.subject` from a singleton to a repeating element, creating a hard JSON shape break for populated R4 instances. The main migration concerns are `subject` array conversion, broader subject/source reference targets, and removal of R4 mode constraints for `entry.deleted`/`entry.date`. The main uncertainty is intent and recommended usage for the relaxed entry-mode semantics because no official narrative diff was supplied.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should handle `List.subject` first: R4 JSON object values need array wrapping for R6, and R6 arrays need cardinality and target checks before down-conversion to R4. Systems should also revisit author/subject target handling and compartment/access-control assumptions because R6 permits broader references. Finally, validators and business rules that encoded R4 `lst-2`/`lst-3` need explicit policy decisions about whether to keep rejecting those combinations locally or accept the R6 relaxation.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural changes because both assigned StructureDefinitions are present and the List differentials make the changed local elements explicit. Confidence is medium for rationale and clinical/business interpretation of constraint relaxation because the analysis did not include official ballot change notes or narrative pages. Terminology confidence is sufficient for List status/mode required bindings, but lower for preferred/example bindings whose external CodeSystems were not all bundled locally in R6.

findings.title: List.subject changed from singleton to repeating, changing JSON shape and generated APIs

semanticText.short: If all resources have the same subject
semanticText.definition: The common subject (or patient) of the resources that are in the list if there is one.
semanticText.comment: Some purely arbitrary lists do not have a common subject, so this is optional.
semanticText.requirements: The primary purpose of listing the subject explicitly is to help with finding the right list.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, `List.subject` could appear at most once. In JSON, a populated singleton is encoded as an object, for example `"subject": {"reference": "Patient/123"}`.

semanticText.short: If all resources have the same subject(s)
semanticText.definition: The common subject(s) (or patient(s)) of the resources that are in the list if there is one (or a set of subjects).
semanticText.comment: Some purely arbitrary lists do not have a common subject, so this is optional. Lists having multiple subjects may raise challenges for systems that base access control or other security considerations on linkages to 'subject'. E.g. if a List is associated with multiple Patient subjects, then it would be nominally part of multiple patient compartments, which might drive access rights.
semanticText.requirements: The primary purpose of listing the subject explicitly is to help with finding the right list.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, `List.subject` is repeating. In JSON, any populated value is encoded as an array, for example `"subject": [{"reference": "Patient/123"}]`.

facts.note: FHIR JSON singleton/repeating encoding changes object vs array shape.

facts.oldValue: If all resources have the same subject
facts.newValue: If all resources have the same subject(s)

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged (`List.subject`), so this is a local cardinality and representation change rather than a rename or move.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a hard wire-format break for JSON instances with a populated `subject`: R4 JSON uses a single object, while R6 JSON requires an array for the same path. Code generators also typically change the property type from `Reference`/nullable to `List<Reference>` or equivalent. R6→R4 is straightforward only when there is exactly one subject and its target is otherwise R4-allowed; multiple subjects cannot be represented in the R4 base element without loss or extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Subject drives discovery, patient compartment membership, authorization, and routing in many implementations. R6 explicitly warns that multiple subjects can challenge access-control assumptions.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow a List to explicitly represent a set of common subjects, including multi-patient or non-patient subject contexts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `List.subject` 0..1 for the first/common subject and add a new optional repeating base element for additional subjects.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of first-class multi-subject Lists is reasonable and is visible in the R6 cardinality and text, including explicit access-control caveats. Changing `List.subject` itself to repeating creates a real JSON and codegen break, but the strongest less-breaking base design would split one subject on the old path and additional subjects on a new path. Because that alternative has material interoperability and safety tradeoffs around a security-sensitive element, the break is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have retained `List.subject` as `0..1` and added a new repeating element such as `List.additionalSubject` for extra common subjects. This would preserve most R4-valid instances and generated APIs for the common single-subject case. The tradeoff is that the same clinical fact would be represented across two same-resource paths; deprecated or parallel representations tend to persist, and generic clients would need clear rules to combine them for search, compartments, authorization, and display. An extension-only approach would be a migration mitigation, not an equivalent base-design alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 JSON for single-subject Lists, but creates duplicate same-resource subject representations that generic search, compartment, and access-control logic must merge.

evidence.detail: R4 `List.subject` has cardinality 0..1 and target profiles Patient, Group, Device, and Location.
evidence.quote: max: 1; targetProfile: Patient | Group | Device | Location

evidence.detail: R6 `List.subject` has cardinality 0..* and target profile Resource.
R6 comments explicitly call out multiple-subject access-control implications.
evidence.quote: Lists having multiple subjects may raise challenges for systems that base access control or other security considerations on linkages to subject.

examples.examplesMd: The R4 example is illustrative of the JSON shape issue: the rest of the resource is minimal. A single allowed subject can be wrapped into a one-item R6 array losslessly; multiple R6 subjects cannot be collapsed into R4 without choosing one, using extensions, or splitting the List.

findings.narrativeMd: `List.subject` keeps the same path but changes from a singleton to a repeating element. In FHIR JSON this is not just a cardinality relaxation: it changes the serialized representation for every populated subject from an object to an array. Existing R4 parsers, generated classes, FHIRPath assumptions, and client code that read `subject.reference` as a single value need changes to handle `subject[0].reference` and potentially multiple values.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A populated R4 JSON instance with `subject` as an object is not valid R6 JSON for a repeating element unless transformed to an array. Conversely, an R6 JSON instance with `subject` as an array is not valid R4 JSON as-is; if the array has exactly one R4-allowed target, it can be converted losslessly to the R4 singleton shape, but arrays with more than one item cannot fit the R4 cardinality.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: During R4→R6 migration, wrap any populated `List.subject` object in a one-item array and update generated model accessors and tests. During R6→R4 conversion, reject, split, or extension-map Lists with more than one subject; do not silently choose the first subject because that can alter compartment and access-control semantics.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The model goal appears to be first-class support for multi-subject Lists. A backward-compatible alternative would have preserved `List.subject` as singleton and added a separate repeating element or extension for additional subjects. That would have avoided the JSON shape break but would also have made multi-subject discovery and generic processing less uniform.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding intentionally separates the singleton-to-array representation break from the separate target-profile widening on the same element.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `List.subject` was an optional singleton, so a populated JSON instance used an object; R6 makes the same path repeating, so the R6 JSON shape is an array even for one subject. That is a real old-valid/new-invalid and generated-API break: an R4 medicine or problem list with `subject: {"reference":"Patient/123"}` needs array wrapping before R6 validation, and R6 multi-subject lists cannot round-trip to the R4 base path. The R6 goal of representing multiple common subjects is coherent, and the required migration for existing single-subject instances is mechanical. Given the R4 artifact's low maturity, this does not look disproportionate enough to require standards redesign.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.subject` max `1`, target profiles Patient, Group, Device, Location.
R6 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.subject` max `*`, target profile Resource, with a comment warning that multiple subjects can challenge subject-based access control.
R4 maturity map: List is FMM 1 and trial-use.

Targeted web check found some implementation relevance, not broad normative reliance: HL7 AU Base R4 AU Medicine List profile describes a patient medicine list and examples serialize `subject` as an R4 singleton object; MuleSoft FHIR R4 List library describes List use for allergies, medications, workflow lists, and patient-specific curated lists.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 List is FMM 1/trial-use, which substantially softens the stability concern. The AU Base and vendor examples show the path can matter in implemented exchanges, but they do not overcome the low-FMM expectation or the mechanical nature of the single-subject migration.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid plus runtime/API/codegen: populated R4 JSON uses an object where R6 expects an array, and generated models change from a nullable/reference property to a collection. There is also R6-to-R4 loss for multiple subjects.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have kept `List.subject` as 0..1 and added a new repeating `additionalSubject`-style element. That would preserve most R4 instances, but it would split one subject concept across two paths and force generic search, compartment, display, and access-control logic to merge them. A FHIR-JSON singleton exception would be even broader and inconsistent with normal repeating-element encoding. The alternatives have material interoperability and security-processing tradeoffs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing report: the hard JSON/codegen break and high reverse-conversion risk are real, but the existing High impact framing gives too little weight to FMM 1/trial-use and to the tradeoffs of the less-breaking alternatives.

findings.title: List.subject target domain widened from four resource types to any Resource

oldState.summary: `List.subject` could reference Patient, Group, Device, or Location.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 constrained `List.subject` to four target profiles, so validators and generated reference-target unions could reject other resource types.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses `Reference(Resource)`, making all concrete resources potential subjects and requiring implementations to handle types that were impossible in base R4.

facts.oldValue: The common subject (or patient) of the resources that are in the list if there is one.
facts.newValue: The common subject(s) (or patient(s)) of the resources that are in the list if there is one (or a set of subjects).

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The unchanged id/path `List.subject` directly identifies the element; only its target profile set and semantic text changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The R4 target set is a subset of `Resource`, so target widening does not make an R4 subject target invalid in R6. It does mean R6 consumers and generated code must handle subject references to resource types that R4 code never expected. R6→R4 conversion is not clean for any subject target outside Patient, Group, Device, or Location.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Subject type and multiplicity commonly feed authorization, compartment routing, and patient-context selection. R6 explicitly warns about access-control challenges for multiple subjects.

justification.inferredGoal: Support Lists whose common subject is not limited to patient/group/device/location contexts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: widening `List.subject` to `Reference(Resource)` preserves the R4 target set, so this target-domain change is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of allowing Lists whose common subject is outside Patient, Group, Device, and Location is reasonable and aligns with the broader R6 List description. The broad `Reference(Resource)` choice weakens static validation and raises access-control concerns, so the rationale is only probably justified. However, because every R4-allowed target remains allowed in R6, the target widening itself does not create an R4-to-R6 instance break; the separate singleton-to-array wire break is covered by the serialization finding.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible alternative is applicable for this finding under the calibration rule because the base target-domain change is a widening that preserves R4-valid subject targets. A narrower base list of added targets, or profile guidance limiting subjects, might reduce arbitrary-target processing and down-conversion gaps, but those choices would constrain the R6 goal rather than preserve additional R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Narrower targets or profile constraints could reduce R6-to-R4 and runtime handling risk, but that is an interoperability/safety tradeoff rather than a backward-compatible alternative for preserving R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 target profiles are Patient, Group, Device, and Location.

examples.examplesMd: `Organization/abc` illustrates a subject target allowed by `Reference(Resource)` in R6 but outside the R4 `List.subject` target set.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 turns `List.subject` into a broad `Reference(Resource)`. This improves flexibility but removes a strong R4 validation constraint and can surprise implementations that map List subject directly to a patient, group, device, or location context. Even after handling the array shape, R6 clients need to branch on arbitrary resource targets.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances that use one of the R4 target types remain target-compatible with R6, subject to the separate array-shape change. R6 instances that use any other target type are valid against the R6 target domain but invalid against the R4 base `List.subject` target constraint unless represented through an extension or profile-specific mapping.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update validators, generated target-type unions, authorization logic, and search/indexing code to allow arbitrary resource targets or to enforce a local profile if the system still requires a narrower set. For R6→R4, reject or extension-map non-R4 targets rather than rewriting them to an imprecise allowed target.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broad target domain was not the only possible design. HL7 could have added a smaller set of likely target profiles or relied on extensions/profiles for uncommon subjects. The chosen base-model flexibility is useful but shifts safety and interoperability checks to implementation guides and business rules.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Review with compartment and search-parameter analyses; broad subjects may alter which patient or organizational contexts a List participates in.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The target-domain change by itself widens `List.subject` from Patient, Group, Device, and Location to any Resource. Every R4-allowed target remains allowed in R6, so this specific finding does not make old instances invalid. Implementers consuming new R6 data may need to handle subject references to resource types that R4 code did not expect, and such instances do not down-convert cleanly to R4, but that is a reverse/new-content concern rather than a breaking R4-to-R6 base compatibility issue. The separate array-shape break is covered by the serialization finding.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.subject` target profiles are Patient, Group, Device, and Location.
R6 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.subject` target profile is Resource.
R6 comment on `List.subject` flags access-control challenges for multiple subjects; that concern is mainly tied to multiplicity and local policy, not to invalidating R4 target references.
R4 maturity map: List is FMM 1 and trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Low FMM further reduces the case for revisiting a pure widening. The production-use evidence found for List does not show that the R4 base target set needs to remain closed for compatibility.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss and possible runtime/API/codegen broadening only: R6 subjects outside the four R4 targets cannot be represented in the R4 base element, but no R4 target becomes invalid in R6.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base design is needed to preserve R4 instances because the change is target widening. A narrower R6 target list or profile-level constraints might improve static validation for some communities, but that would constrain the R6 goal rather than avoid an R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing High impact judgment for this finding. I agree that broad targets can create reverse-conversion and policy work, but the independent path-level assessment finds no meaningful R4-to-R6 compatibility problem from the target widening itself.

findings.title: List.source author targets expanded to Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group

oldState.summary: `List.source` could reference Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, or Device.

semanticText.short: Who and/or what defined the list contents (aka Author)
semanticText.definition: The entity responsible for deciding what the contents of the list were. Where the list was created by a human, this is the same as the author of the list.
semanticText.comment: The primary source is the entity that made the decisions what items are in the list. This may be software or user.
semanticText.requirements: Allows follow-up as well as context.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 constrained the source/author to individual, role, patient, or device actors.

newState.summary: `List.source` also allows Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group.

semanticText.short: Who and/or what defined the list contents (aka Author)
semanticText.definition: The entity responsible for deciding what the contents of the list were. Where the list was created by a human, this is the same as the author of the list.
semanticText.comment: The primary source is the entity that made the decisions what items are in the list. This may be software or user.
semanticText.requirements: Allows follow-up as well as context.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 preserves cardinality and prose but broadens the allowed author/source actor types.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path remain `List.source`; R6 adds target profiles without changing cardinality or prose.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a pure widening of reference targets. Existing R4 source references remain allowed in R6. R6 Lists whose source is Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, or Group cannot be represented in the R4 base `List.source` element without extension/profile support or loss of the source actor.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The source/author can be used for accountability, workflow routing, provenance-like displays, and follow-up. Dropping or coercing a disallowed R6 source during down-conversion can misattribute responsibility.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow organizations, care teams, groups, and related persons to be explicit authors/sources of Lists.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: R6 only adds target profiles to `List.source`, preserving all R4-valid source references.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The added Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group source targets fit the existing definition of `List.source` as the entity responsible for list contents and represent common authorship/accountability cases. Since the cardinality and JSON shape are unchanged and all R4 source targets remain valid, the base R6 design is justified from an R4-to-R6 compatibility perspective.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible alternative is applicable because this is target widening that preserves R4 instances. Extensions or profile-specific allowances could have represented the new source actors for some implementations, but that would be a migration or profiling strategy rather than a base-design alternative needed to avoid R4-to-R6 breakage.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The added targets create R6-to-R4 mapping gaps and generated-code updates, but they do not require a less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R4 target profiles are Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, and Device.
R6 adds Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group to the allowed source targets.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows an R6 source target newly allowed by the base StructureDefinition. A local R4 profile could choose to allow it, but the R4 core target set does not.

findings.narrativeMd: `List.source` retains the same cardinality and meaning, but R6 allows four additional author/source resource types. This is not a hard R4→R6 break, but it matters for generated target-type enums, validators, authorization/audit displays, and R6→R4 conversion.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with a Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, or Device source remains structurally compatible with R6. An R6 instance using Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, or Group as the source is invalid against R4 core target constraints unless the data is moved to an extension or constrained by a compatible profile.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update source-target validation and generated reference wrappers to include the four added targets. For down-conversion, preserve the actor via an extension or reject the conversion if the receiving R4 system cannot accept non-core targets.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is a reasonable base-model widening for author/source accountability. It could have been less disruptive by using extensions, but that would hide the source from generic processing and make common institutional authorship less interoperable.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group as allowed `List.source` targets while preserving the R4 Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, and Device targets and the same 0..1 wire shape. Existing R4 instances remain valid at this path. R6 instances using one of the new author/source actors may not fit the R4 base model, and strongly typed generated code may broaden its accepted target union, but those are expected effects of an additive target widening rather than a concerning R4-to-R6 break.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.source` targets Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, and Device.
R6 StructureDefinition-List.json: `List.source` also allows Organization, RelatedPerson, CareTeam, and Group.
HL7 AU Base R4 AU Medicine List used an extension for RelatedPerson authorship instead of `List.source`, illustrating that at least one R4 IG had to work around the narrower source target set.
R4 maturity map: List is FMM 1 and trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use softens any stability objection, and the change is widening rather than restrictive. The low maturity plus plausible authorship/accountability use cases support treating this as acceptable.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss only, with minor runtime/API/codegen broadening: new R6 source targets may not map to R4 core `List.source`, but all R4 source targets remain valid in R6.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base design is applicable because R4 instances are preserved. Keeping the new actors in extensions or profiles would reduce base-model breadth, but it would also keep common source/accountability cases out of generic processing and would not improve R4-to-R6 compatibility.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing report: the reverse-mapping gap is real, but the Medium impact framing overstates the R4-to-R6 concern for a pure additive target change.

findings.title: R4 mode-dependent entry constraints lst-2 and lst-3 were removed

oldState.summary: R4 had local error invariants `lst-2` and `lst-3` tying `entry.deleted` to `mode=changes` and `entry.date` to `mode=working`.

constraints.human: The deleted flag can only be used if the mode of the list is "changes"
An entry date can only be used if the mode of the list is "working"

semanticText.comment: R4 comments on `entry.deleted` and `entry.flag` also stated that deleted/flag usage was limited to `mode=changes`.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 validators rejected Lists with `entry.deleted` unless `mode` was `changes`, and rejected Lists with `entry.date` unless `mode` was `working`.

newState.summary: R6 keeps `lst-1` but no longer carries `lst-2` or `lst-3`; the R6 comments also remove the explicit mode restriction for deleted/flag.

constraints.human: A list can only have an emptyReason if it is empty

semanticText.comment: R6 `entry.deleted` still explains deleted display/modifier semantics, but no longer says it can only be used when `mode=changes`.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 no longer has computable root constraints preventing `entry.deleted` in working/snapshot Lists or `entry.date` in snapshot/changes Lists.

facts.oldValue: Both flag and deleted can only be used if the List.mode is "changes".
Deleted can only be used if the List.mode is "changes".

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The changed constraints are local List root invariants in the R4 differential. R6 keeps the same root element and only retains `lst-1`, so `lst-2` and `lst-3` are true removals rather than inherited base changes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a relaxation, so R4-valid instances remain valid with respect to these constraints in R6. The risk is the reverse: R6 can now accept combinations that R4 core validators rejected. Runtime code that relied on `mode` to decide when `deleted` or `date` could appear may misinterpret R6 data.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: `entry.deleted` is a modifier indicating an item is no longer part of the list. Accepting it outside the R4 `changes` mode can affect clinical/workflow displays and list completeness assumptions.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit entry deletion markers and entry dates in more List modes, or remove constraints considered too restrictive.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: removing `lst-2` and `lst-3` is a validation relaxation, so R4-valid Lists are not made invalid in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The StructureDefinitions clearly show that the mode-dependent hard constraints were removed, but the supplied primary inputs do not explain the ballot rationale. The inferred goal of permitting `entry.deleted` and `entry.date` in more modes may be reasonable, yet the removed `deleted` rule involved a modifier element with display and workflow consequences. Without narrative or issue-history evidence, the reasonableness of removing the hard constraints from the base resource cannot be assessed confidently.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible alternative is applicable for the compact R4-to-R6 judgment because this is not an R4-to-R6 validation break; it is mainly an R6-to-R4 and runtime semantic concern. R6 could have retained warning-level guidance or recommended mode-specific profiles to preserve interoperability cues, but ordinary migration guidance or local profile policy is not the same as a less-breaking base R6 design for existing R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Warning-level invariants or profile guidance could reduce semantic risk, but they would not be a backward-compatible alternative for preserving R4 instances; retaining hard constraints would fail the inferred R6 relaxation goal.

evidence.detail: R4 required `entry.deleted` to be absent unless `mode` is `changes`.
R4 required `entry.date` to be absent unless `mode` is `working`.
R6 List root keeps only `lst-1`; `lst-2` and `lst-3` are absent.
R4 `List.entry.deleted` declares condition `lst-2`; the R6 element does not.

examples.examplesMd: The example is valid against the R6 structure with respect to the removed `lst-2` constraint but violates R4 `lst-2` because `mode` is `working` and `entry.deleted` is present. A similar example can be made for `mode=changes` with `entry.date`, violating R4 `lst-3`.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 removes two local List invariants that used `mode` to constrain entry metadata. This is not an R4→R6 validation break; it is a conformance relaxation. The migration risk is that R6 data can now combine `mode`, `entry.deleted`, and `entry.date` in ways that R4 validators and many R4-era business rules considered invalid.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid Lists do not become invalid because these constraints were removed. R6-valid Lists using `entry.deleted` outside `mode=changes` or `entry.date` outside `mode=working` are not R4-core-valid. Strict validators, FHIRPath rules, and generated validation annotations that still include `lst-2`/`lst-3` will reject such R6 content.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Decide whether the receiving system will accept the R6 relaxation or retain R4-compatible policy as a local profile. For R6→R4, either reject these combinations, remove the incompatible entry metadata with explicit loss accounting, or transform to a profile/extension that the R4 receiver understands. Test mode combinations for `working`, `snapshot`, and `changes` with and without `deleted` and `date`.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: If the goal was broader use of entry metadata, a warning-level invariant or profile-based relaxation would have been more backward-compatible than removing the hard constraints from the base resource. The tradeoff is that retaining warnings may continue to discourage valid R6 use cases.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Because `entry.deleted` is a modifier, human review should confirm that local UI, reconciliation, and completeness logic does not silently treat deleted entries as active list members.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 had hard invariants tying `entry.deleted` to `mode = changes` and `entry.date` to `mode = working`; R6 removes those constraints and related condition text. This is a validation relaxation, so R4-valid Lists remain valid with respect to these rules. New R6 combinations may be rejected by R4 validators or by local profiles that keep the old policy, and consumers still need to honor `entry.deleted` as a modifier, but the change does not create an old-valid/new-invalid break. Without stronger evidence of production reliance on the exact R4 invariants, the low-FMM context makes this a reverse/semantic policy concern rather than a standards revisit issue.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-List.json root constraints include `lst-2` (`mode = 'changes' or entry.deleted.empty()`) and `lst-3` (`mode = 'working' or entry.date.empty()`).
R6 StructureDefinition-List.json root constraints retain `lst-1` but omit `lst-2` and `lst-3`.
R4 `List.entry.deleted` condition includes `lst-2`; R6 `List.entry.deleted` has no such condition but remains a modifier explaining deleted display semantics.
R4 and R6 `List.mode` text both say mode is a modifier because a change list must not be misunderstood as a complete list.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use reduces the stability burden for relaxing mode-dependent constraints. The modifier nature of `entry.deleted` keeps this worth noticing, but it is not enough to treat a non-restrictive change as a material R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss and semantic/conformance relaxation: R6 permits combinations R4 rejected, but no R4-valid instance is newly invalid in R6.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have retained the old rules as warnings or moved the relaxation to profiles, but that would preserve conformance pressure rather than preserve R4 instances. Retaining the hard constraints would fail the apparent R6 goal of allowing broader entry metadata use. Local profiles can still reimpose the R4 policy when needed.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing Medium impact and human-review emphasis for R4-to-R6 compatibility. I agree with the factual finding that the constraints were removed, but independently judge the result as a low-FMM relaxation with primarily reverse-direction effects.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The R6 `List` StructureDefinition exists at the expected path and keeps the same canonical URL, id, name, kind, concrete/abstract flag, type, baseDefinition, and derivation. Publication maturity changed and is recorded as a notable non-breaking change.
The local List differential has the same element ids in R4 and R6; no local List element was added, removed, renamed, moved, split, or merged.

`List.status` and `List.mode` remain required bindings to ValueSets with the same canonical systems and the same local required codes. `List.code`, `List.orderedBy`, `List.entry.flag`, and `List.emptyReason` keep the same binding strengths and ValueSet canonicals; full expansions were not available for every external terminology system in R6.
No fixed value, pattern, or default value constraints were found on local List elements in either version.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraints were found that changed between R4 and R6.

Local modifier flags remain stable for `List.status`, `List.mode`, and `List.entry.deleted`. The semantic constraint removal affecting `entry.deleted` is captured separately as a value-constraint finding.
Local List summary flags remain materially unchanged for the List-specific elements. Inherited summary-flag changes on base elements are out of scope.
No local slicing rules or slice definitions were present on `List` elements in the compared StructureDefinitions.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: List publication maturity increased from draft/trial-use/FMM 1 to active/normative/FMM 4
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Publication status and maturity metadata do not by themselves change instance validation or wire format. They are nevertheless important because downstream governance may treat normative content as less flexible than trial-use content.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Review local policies that gate adoption or change control based on standards status or FMM. This metadata change may affect governance even though it is not an instance-level break.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Required List.status and List.mode bindings point to R6-versioned ValueSets with unchanged local code sets
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The required bindings still compose from `http://hl7.org/fhir/list-status` and `http://hl7.org/fhir/list-mode`, and the local CodeSystem concepts for `current`, `retired`, `entered-in-error`, `working`, `snapshot`, and `changes` are unchanged apart from minor display/definition text and status/version metadata.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Systems that compare binding URLs including explicit version strings should expect `|4.0.1` to become `|6.0.0-ballot4`, but code validation against the local required code sets should not reject previously valid codes on this basis.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds XDS mapping metadata for List, subject, and source
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Mapping metadata does not affect base instance validation or serialization. It can matter for tooling that generates transforms or documentation from StructureDefinition mappings.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Transformation tooling may now see XDS mappings such as `SubmissionSet.patientId` and `SubmissionSet.author`; review generated transforms if mapping metadata is consumed automatically.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: List root definition now includes examples such as facility and organization lists
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The root definition text is broader, but the material structural effects are captured in the `subject`, `source`, and constraint findings. The wording alone does not invalidate R4 instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The broader description may signal intended use beyond classic patient-centered clinical lists and should be considered when designing profiles and access-control policy.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited snapshot differences such as `language` binding strength/value set and `dom-3` expression changes appear on `List` but are base-artifact issues and should be assessed in the DomainResource/Resource reports.

`List.subject` and `List.source` target domains changed locally. SearchParameter target lists and compartment behavior should be reviewed separately because they affect query compatibility and access-control indexing but are outside this resource StructureDefinition report.

followUpDependencies.nameOrUrl: THO CodeSystems for list-empty-reason, list-order, and list-example-use-codes
followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Some terminology systems used by preferred/example List bindings were present as local R4 CodeSystems but not bundled as local R6 CodeSystems in the core package. A terminology-server or THO package comparison would improve expansion confidence.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4→R6 diff narrative or ballot issue history was used. Structural conclusions are high-confidence, but rationale and intended migration patterns are inferred from the computable definitions.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review official HL7 change notes, Jira tickets, or generated spec diff pages for `List`.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The human narrative specification pages were not reviewed. This limits confidence in semantic interpretation of multiple subjects and relaxed entry-mode constraints beyond the StructureDefinition comments.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the R4 and R6 List resource narrative pages and examples.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology comparison was based on local ValueSet compose definitions and local CodeSystems where available, not live terminology expansions. This is unlikely to affect the main required-binding conclusions for `List.status` and `List.mode`, but it limits confidence for preferred/example bindings.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run terminology expansions against matching R4 and R6/THO terminology packages.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Profiles, implementation guides, SearchParameters, and compartment definitions were not analyzed as findings. They may amplify or mitigate the impact of broader `subject` and `source` references.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Analyze List SearchParameters, compartment membership rules, and common implementation-guide profiles separately.
